title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction
authors: Makoto Takamoto, Chaitanya Sampara, Viktor Zaverkin, Daniel Oñoro-Rubio, Mathias Niepert
abstract: It is well established that molecular substructures can contribute unequally to chemical and physical properties, with specific motifs or side chains often playing dominant roles. Fragment-based representations have therefore emerged as an effective strategy for incorporating chemically meaningful inductive biases, as exemplified by molecular fingerprints and fragment-based attention mechanisms. However, many existing fragmentation-based machine learning methods rely on predefined chemical rules, which may yield suboptimal fragmentation for previously unseen or chemically unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations. To address these limitations, we formulate molecular fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization problem inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters is not fixed a priori but emerges from the specified radius, and propose a geometry-based fragmentation method that partitions arbitrary molecular or material structures using largely geometric information, without relying on predefined chemical fragmentation rules. The method provides flexible control over fragment size, enabling the construction of multiscale fragment representations for scale-adaptive modeling. Building on this framework, we develop a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structural information and incorporate it into a multimodal machine learning model combining p-SMILES representations with three-dimensional (3D) conformational information. Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show that incorporating 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based exclusively on p-SMILES representations. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses further provide insights into the physical relevance of the learned representations.

infographic.key_insight: Geometry-based molecular fragmentation enables multiscale polymer representations without predefined chemical fragmentation rules.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining polymer sequence and 3D structural information can improve property prediction while highlighting potentially influential molecular regions.
method: Formulate fragmentation as radius-constrained optimization inspired by k-center clustering, letting fragment count emerge from the radius.
Vary the radius to construct multiscale fragments and integrate them through geometric fragment-based attention.
Combine p-SMILES representations with 3D conformational information in a multimodal prediction model.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a benchmark polymer dataset, adding 3D conformational information improved prediction accuracy for several properties over p-SMILES-only models; explainability analyses explored the representations' physical relevance.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify gains or establish robustness to conformer choice and fragmentation radius.
infographic.paper_title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction

title: Inverse design of superconductors and semiconductors with differentiable foundation models
authors: Cristóbal Méndez, Justin Tahmassebpur, Tomás A. Arias
abstract: Designing a crystal for a target property requires choosing its elements, stoichiometry, and atomic structure together, yet gradients exist only for the continuous structural variables. We introduce differentiable Equiformer fast effective-atom theory (DEFEAT), which lets a pretrained EquiformerV3 foundation model accept continuous species weights and site occupancies without retraining on fractional data, thereby enabling gradient-based materials optimization. Gradients from fine-tuned property models and a machine-learned energy penalty then guide updates to composition, atom count, atomic positions, and lattice vectors in a single optimization. In a search for phonon-mediated superconductors, density-functional perturbation theory on 45 structurally novel designs gives isotropic Allen-Dynes critical temperatures above 10 K for 39; the highest is 24.0 K for ZrTiNb2CN3, and H4LiPd3 (23.2 K) lies on the static DFT hull. In searches for photovoltaic absorbers, SCAN calculations confirm ten novel crystal structures with band gaps within 20% of a 1.34 eV target on their respective raw or empirically corrected scales, all within 70 meV/atom of the DFT hull, and show that the systematic gap error of the training functional propagates into the designs unless the objective corrects for it. Quasiharmonic free energies from machine-learned potentials further show that finite-temperature competition with solid phases can reorder candidates relative to the static hull.

infographic.key_insight: DEFEAT makes element identity and site occupancy differentiable, enabling joint gradient-based design of crystal composition, atom count, atomic positions, and lattice.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables targeted searches for superconductors and photovoltaic absorbers while incorporating an energy penalty to discourage unstable designs.
method: Extend a pretrained EquiformerV3 model to continuous species weights and site occupancies without fractional-data retraining.
Combine gradients from fine-tuned property models with a machine-learned energy penalty.
Validate candidates using first-principles calculations and assess finite-temperature stability with machine-learned potentials.
infographic.evidence_signal: DFPT yields Allen–Dynes critical temperatures above 10 K for 39 of 45 structurally novel designs; SCAN confirms ten novel absorber structures within 20% of a 1.34 eV target on raw or corrected gap scales, all within 70 meV/atom of the DFT hull.
infographic.watch_item: Training-functional band-gap bias propagates into designs unless corrected in the objective, and finite-temperature phase competition can change static-hull rankings.
infographic.paper_title: Inverse design of superconductors and semiconductors with differentiable foundation models

title: ZeoBench: A Benchmark for Self-Supervised Learning on 3D Zeolite Representations
authors: Aaron Sun, Yachan Liu, Ping Yang, Peng Bai, Subhransu Maji
abstract: Zeolites are an important class of porous crystalline materials with broad applications in gas storage, separations, and catalysis. Although hundreds of thousands of experimentally realized and hypothetical zeolite structures are known, identifying materials optimized for a target application remains challenging because property labels are expensive to obtain and available only for limited structure-molecule pairs. While prior work has demonstrated that 3D neural representations can predict zeolite properties effectively, it remains unclear which representation-learning strategies are most effective in the low-data regime relevant to materials discovery. We present ZeoBench, a benchmark for self-supervised learning on dense 3D representations of all-silica zeolites, and evaluate the resulting features on six existing downstream adsorption-property prediction tasks, across a range of training set sizes. Our study compares self-supervised 3D pretraining on volumetric zeolite data, adaptations of image-pretrained 2D ConvNets and vision transformers to 3D via multiview and channel-inflation strategies, and 3D ConvNets pretrained on out-of-domain volumetric datasets, alongside hand-crafted descriptors and supervised baselines. Using our pretraining and evaluation framework, we find self-supervised 3D representations outperform existing methods and achieve state-of-the-art performance across both in-domain label regimes and for the unseen domain of metal organic frameworks. Learned representations consistently outperform hand-crafted descriptors, and convolutional architectures are generally more effective than vision transformers in this setting. These results establish ZeoBench as a practical benchmark for 3D representation learning in zeolites and provide guidance for data-limited adsorption property prediction.

infographic.key_insight: Self-supervised learning on dense 3D zeolite representations achieves state-of-the-art adsorption-property prediction, including transfer to metal–organic frameworks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Better predictions with limited property labels could help prioritize porous materials for gas storage, separations, and catalysis.
method: Pretrain self-supervised models on volumetric representations of all-silica zeolites.
Compare 3D pretraining with adapted image-pretrained models and out-of-domain volumetric pretraining.
Evaluate against hand-crafted descriptors and supervised baselines across training-set sizes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covers six existing adsorption-property prediction tasks across training-set sizes, with learned features consistently outperforming hand-crafted descriptors and convolutional architectures generally outperforming vision transformers.
infographic.watch_item: Pretraining focuses on all-silica zeolites; transfer to metal–organic frameworks does not establish generalization across all porous-material chemistries.
infographic.paper_title: ZeoBench: A Benchmark for Self-Supervised Learning on 3D Zeolite Representations

title: Native point defects in rock-salt and wurtzite MnSe: formation energies across the growth window and spin splitting in the A-type order
authors: Tomás Rojas Solorzano, Dale Igram
abstract: Manganese selenide grows both as rock-salt $α$-MnSe, a type-II antiferromagnet, and as metastable wurtzite w-MnSe, whose magnetic order has not been measured. We compute the neutral Mn and Se vacancies and the two antisites of both polymorphs with density functional theory plus a linear-response Hubbard $U$, between the Se-rich limit bounded by MnSe$_2$ and the Mn-rich limit set by the measured formation enthalpy. In $α$-MnSe the Mn vacancy is lowest over most of the window (0.92 eV under Se-rich conditions), consistent with its p-type conduction. In w-MnSe, the Se antisite is lowest under Se-rich conditions, narrowly in the A-type order and clearly in the stripe order, and the Se vacancy is lowest under Mn-rich conditions. The Se vacancy has nearly the same formation energy in both polymorphs, whereas defects that change the number of Mn atoms differ by 0.4-1.1 eV, although DFT+$U$ places wurtzite below rock salt, contrary to experiment. A spin-degenerate stripe order lies 14 meV per formula unit below the altermagnetic A-type order of w-MnSe, and the formation energies shift between these orders by up to 0.24 eV, most for the Mn vacancy. Three of the four defects leave an uncompensated moment of 3-5 $μ_\mathrm{B}$. In the A-type order, band unfolding shows that the sign-reversing splitting of the most strongly split band, about 230 meV and 3 eV below the valence-band maximum, keeps its peak height within the 8% scatter of the analysis at 3% defects, while points on its shoulders move by up to about 70 meV. Band-edge states are not resolved.

infographic.key_insight: Native-defect stability in MnSe depends on crystal structure, growth conditions and magnetic order, while 3% defects largely preserve the peak spin splitting studied in A-type wurtzite MnSe.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Growth chemistry offers a route to favor particular defects, with Mn vacancies dominant across most of the rock-salt growth window and consistent with p-type conduction.
method: DFT with linear-response Hubbard U for neutral Mn and Se vacancies and both antisites.
Formation-energy comparison across Se-rich and Mn-rich limits in rock-salt and wurtzite MnSe.
Magnetic-order comparison and band unfolding to assess defect-induced spin-splitting changes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The rock-salt Mn vacancy costs 0.92 eV at the Se-rich limit; wurtzite stripe order lies 14 meV per formula unit below A-type order, whose approximately 230 meV peak splitting remains within 8% analysis scatter at 3% defects.
infographic.watch_item: DFT+U incorrectly favors wurtzite over rock salt, wurtzite magnetic order remains experimentally unmeasured, and band-edge spin splitting is unresolved.
infographic.paper_title: Native point defects in rock-salt and wurtzite MnSe: formation energies across the growth window and spin splitting in the A-type order

title: SteelAgent: LLM-Orchestrated, Physics-Informed Steel Property Prediction with Audited Generalization and Calibrated Uncertainty
authors: Aleksandr Volkov, Roman Sultimov, Mikhail Kuzin, Yury Maximov
abstract: Steel property models can perform well on random test splits even when they extrapolate poorly to unfamiliar alloys. SteelAgent couples metallurgical descriptors and machine-learning models with a language-model interface for property prediction, uncertainty reporting and inverse design. We examine how the choice of held-out unit changes the conclusions drawn from SteelBench tensile-strength evaluations. For gradient boosting, pooled out-of-fold $R^2$ fell from 0.859 on a random split to 0.113 when steel families were held out. Empirical coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals ranged from 91.0% under random splitting to 37.6% on held-out sources. The effect of physics-derived features depended on the evaluation. They increased gradient-boosting $R^2$ by 0.2534 in a 17-family holdout analysis and decreased it by 0.358 in a separate four-grade laboratory analysis. We report group-level errors and a synthetic regression experiment illustrating how calibration can deteriorate on held-out groups. These results motivate reporting the evaluation population alongside a property estimate or compliance score.

infographic.key_insight: SteelAgent’s apparent accuracy and uncertainty reliability drop sharply when evaluation holds out unfamiliar steel families or data sources instead of random samples.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Steel property estimates used for alloy screening or compliance decisions should report the evaluation population and uncertainty performance on relevant held-out groups.
method: Combine metallurgical descriptors and machine-learning models with an LLM interface for prediction, uncertainty reporting and inverse design.
Audit generalization using random, steel-family and source holdouts.
Compare physics-derived features across evaluations and examine calibration with a synthetic regression experiment.
infographic.evidence_signal: On SteelBench tensile-strength evaluations, gradient-boosting pooled out-of-fold R² fell from 0.859 with random splitting to 0.113 with family holdouts; nominal 90% interval coverage was 91.0% under random splitting versus 37.6% on held-out sources.
infographic.watch_item: Physics-derived features were not uniformly beneficial: gradient-boosting R² increased by 0.2534 in a 17-family holdout analysis but decreased by 0.358 in a separate four-grade laboratory analysis.
infographic.paper_title: SteelAgent: LLM-Orchestrated, Physics-Informed Steel Property Prediction with Audited Generalization and Calibrated Uncertainty

title: Spectral symmetry fingerprints in equivariant representations
authors: Jiacheng Cen, Anyi Li, Ning Lin, Zihe Wang, Ji-Rong Wen, Wenbing Huang
abstract: Symmetry governs the organization of physical structures, while symmetry breaking reveals their transformations. In geometric deep learning, symmetry imposes rank constraints on equivariant representations, limiting the expressive capacity of equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs). Here we show that these constraints can instead be exploited: the singular-value spectra of equivariant representations provide a unified fingerprint of structural symmetry. We introduce spectral symmetry fingerprints (SymFP), which enable discrete point-group identification through rank-template matching and continuous symmetry analysis by quantifying spectral energy beyond target rank constraints. SymFP is orientation invariant and architecture agnostic, enabling a parameter-free GNN implementation. Its spectra can be reused across multiple target groups, and the resulting leakage scores satisfy subgroup monotonicity. Across synthetic structures, molecules, coordination complexes and large biological assemblies, SymFP accurately identifies point groups, tracks controlled symmetry breaking and reveals local and degree-resolved symmetry changes that can be obscured by global geometric measures. These results establish the spectral structure of equivariant representations as a general framework for characterizing symmetry across physical systems.

infographic.key_insight: Singular-value spectra of equivariant representations provide orientation-invariant fingerprints for identifying structural symmetry and quantifying symmetry breaking.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SymFP could support symmetry-aware analysis of crystals, molecules and complex assemblies, including local changes that global geometric measures may miss.
method: Extract singular-value spectra from equivariant representations, including a parameter-free GNN implementation.
Identify discrete point groups by matching spectral ranks to symmetry templates.
Quantify symmetry breaking through spectral energy beyond target rank constraints, reusing spectra across target groups.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports accurate point-group identification and tracking of controlled, local and degree-resolved symmetry changes across synthetic structures, molecules, coordination complexes and large biological assemblies.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify numerical rank thresholds or robustness to measurement noise, both important for practical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Spectral symmetry fingerprints in equivariant representations

title: An All-Atom Model of the Resorcinol-Formaldehyde Aerogel Skeleton from DFT and Molecular Dynamics: Validation and Iron Incorporation
authors: Shoeb Athar, Jérémy Guazzagaloppa, Philippe Jund
abstract: Resorcinol-formaldehyde (RF) aerogels are lightweight, ultra-porous thermal superinsulators whose complex amorphous structure has not yet been described at the all-atom level. Here, we build an all-atom model of the RF aerogel skeleton by combining density functional theory (DFT) and classical molecular dynamics (MD), validate it against experimental infrared and density measurements, and use it to study the incorporation of iron dopants. The RF base unit was optimized with Gaussian, DMol$^{3}$ and SIESTA, and its calculated infrared spectrum agreed with experiment. Comparing classical force fields with DFT for branched systems of two to four base units (140-278 atoms) led to the choice of COMPASS II. A 15,012-atom system of 54 branched RF units, not cross-linked to each other, aggregated into a single cluster in the canonical (NVT) ensemble and reached an equilibrium density of 1.296 g.cm$^{-3}$ in the isobaric-isothermal (NPT) ensemble, in agreement with the experimental skeletal density (1.3 g.cm$^{-3}$). Then, 5 wt$\%$ iron (109 atoms) was added to the equilibrated structure: during 1 ns of NPT simulation, the fraction of iron atoms embedded in the skeleton rose from 63$\%$ to 71$\%$, and the Fe-C radial distribution function peaked at 3 Å. The model thus provides an experimentally supported starting point for screening fillers and dopants in RF gels, with prospective application to their thermoelectric functionalization, which we have previously demonstrated experimentally with basalt and PANOX fibres. Future extensions could address skeleton properties relevant to thermal insulation and the pyrolysis of RF gels into carbon and metal-doped carbon aerogels.

infographic.key_insight: A DFT-informed, all-atom model reproduces key experimental features of the resorcinol-formaldehyde aerogel skeleton and enables simulation of iron incorporation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model provides a starting point for screening fillers and dopants for RF aerogels, including prospective thermoelectric functionalization.
method: Optimize the RF base unit with DFT and compare its infrared spectrum with experiment.
Benchmark classical force fields against DFT for branched RF structures and select COMPASS II.
Equilibrate a 15,012-atom skeleton using NVT/NPT molecular dynamics, then simulate 5 wt% iron addition.
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculated infrared spectra agreed with experiment, simulated skeletal density was 1.296 versus 1.3 g/cm³ experimentally, and embedded iron increased from 63% to 71% over 1 ns.
infographic.watch_item: The model aggregates RF units without inter-unit cross-links; longer-term dopant stability and functional properties remain to be validated.
infographic.paper_title: An All-Atom Model of the Resorcinol-Formaldehyde Aerogel Skeleton from DFT and Molecular Dynamics: Validation and Iron Incorporation

title: Physics Informed Priors for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials with Uncertainty Quantification
authors: George I. Simmons, Thomas D. Swinburne, Thomas Hudson, James R. Kermode
abstract: Standard uncertainty quantification methods for machine learning interatomic potentials often fail to quantify the effects of model misspecification despite its prominence as a source of error. To combat this, misspecification-aware uncertainty schemes have been gaining attention, pointwise optimal parameter set regression (POPS-Regression) among them. However, no guarantees on the physicality of the posterior distribution are given and uncertainty estimates can be conservative compared to the true error. To combat this, we present a model misspecification aware scheme that builds on POPS-Regression by allowing users to specify physical priors that are enforced across the obtained ensemble of models. This allows the user to incorporate misspecification-aware uncertainties without compromising on physical properties. The scheme is applicable to any physical quantity that can be represented by a convex set of parameters and so is robust for a wide variety of static properties which can help inform dynamical simulations. Here, we demonstrate the scheme for phononic vibrations and elastic properties. The scheme is also applied to both linear and message-passing neural network potentials by exploiting the linearity available in both architectures; for neural network potentials we approximate the readout layer as a linear model based on fixed non-linear features. The versatility of the method provides an alternative to hand-crafted or active learning approaches to data-set construction to correct physical failures by adding data thus reducing the computational overhead for designing potentials for specific applications.

infographic.key_insight: Adding convex physical priors to POPS-Regression enables misspecification-aware uncertainty estimates while enforcing specified physical properties across the model ensemble.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce the need for costly additional training data to correct physical failures in interatomic potentials designed for specific applications.
method: Extend POPS-Regression with physical constraints expressible as convex sets of model parameters.
Enforce these constraints across the uncertainty ensemble.
Apply to linear potentials and fixed-feature linear readouts of message-passing neural networks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports demonstrations involving phononic vibrations and elastic properties for both linear and message-passing neural network potentials, without quantitative performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees cover only specified convex physical constraints; the neural-network treatment fixes nonlinear features and approximates the readout as linear.
infographic.paper_title: Physics Informed Priors for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials with Uncertainty Quantification

title: Jackknife-conformal uncertainty for linear ACE potentials: calibrated forces and silicon properties compared with Bayesian and POPS baselines
authors: James R. Kermode
abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials are misspecified, so Bayesian posterior variances understate their errors. For linear atomic cluster expansion (ACE) potentials we derive calibrated uncertainties from one misspecification-robust parameter covariance, the delete-one-configuration jackknife. Scaled by one conformal quantile from a held-out part of the training set, it gives per-atom force uncertainties close to their target coverage on held-out silicon data and on cracks left out of the fit; screw dislocations left out are under-covered by the smaller of the two models. With one scale fitted to the forces of a held-out test split, the same parameter distribution is propagated to 21 properties of silicon, from elastic constants to defect and surface energies, by implicit differentiation through each relaxation and by committees, and is tested against density functional theory (DFT) without tuning on any property. For a smaller and a larger model the intervals cover most properties, and the larger model's are about 4 times tighter. The Bayesian posterior with one calibrated scale has the wrong shape: it covers fewer properties and has far lower joint evidence. Pointwise optimal parameter sets (POPS), once their hypercube is numerically defined, performs comparably on the properties, but its per-atom force regions are not calibrated to a target (0.95 and 0.84 at a nominal 0.90). Where the jackknife fails is relaxed point defects, whose training cells are all hot snapshots: a bias that every configuration shares is invisible to a jackknife, but it can be measured from the training labels, and as a discrepancy term, devised after the property results were seen, it brings the coverage close to nominal.

infographic.key_insight: Delete-one-configuration jackknife covariance with conformal scaling gives linear ACE potentials more reliable uncertainty estimates than a calibrated Bayesian posterior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Calibrated force and property intervals can help engineers judge the reliability of silicon simulations involving elasticity, surfaces, cracks, and defects.
method: Estimate parameter covariance by leaving out one training configuration at a time.
Apply a held-out conformal scale to calibrate per-atom force uncertainty.
Propagate parameter uncertainty to relaxed silicon properties using implicit differentiation and committees.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests covered held-out silicon forces, excluded cracks and screw dislocations, and 21 DFT-referenced properties; the larger model produced property intervals about four times tighter, while POPS force coverage was 0.95 and 0.84 at a nominal 0.90.
infographic.watch_item: Jackknife uncertainty misses bias shared across training configurations: relaxed point-defect coverage needed a discrepancy correction devised after inspecting property results.
infographic.paper_title: Jackknife-conformal uncertainty for linear ACE potentials: calibrated forces and silicon properties compared with Bayesian and POPS baselines

title: From local learning to global electronic properties in large-scale systems
authors: Yu Cheng, Zhichang Fu, Yechen Chen, Yonggang Li, Weiqing Zhou, Shengjun Yuan
abstract: Machine learning from local atomic environments offers an efficient route to electronic structure, but evaluating global electronic properties in large systems remains computationally demanding. Here we combine real space charge density learning with stochastic propagation using Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians constructed from the predicted densities. The framework avoids target system self-consistent iterations and explicit diagonalization, while hierarchical blocking enables dense grid inference within limited GPU memory. We demonstrate density of states calculations for one million Si atoms and optical and transport calculations for over one hundred thousand atoms, without training separate models for each property. This framework extends the practical scale of electronic structure calculations within Kohn-Sham DFT, opening opportunities to investigate how atomic structure governs electronic, optical and transport properties at length scales relevant to real materials and devices.

infographic.key_insight: Learning local charge densities and using stochastic Kohn–Sham propagation enables global electronic-property calculations at million-atom scale without target-system self-consistent iterations or explicit diagonalization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework connects atomic structure to electronic, optical and transport properties at scales relevant to materials and devices without separate models for each property.
method: Predict real-space charge density from local atomic environments.
Construct Kohn–Sham Hamiltonians from predicted densities and evaluate properties through stochastic propagation.
Use hierarchical blocking for dense-grid inference within limited GPU memory.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports density-of-states calculations for one million silicon atoms and optical and transport calculations for systems exceeding 100,000 atoms.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify prediction errors or stochastic convergence, leaving accuracy and sampling requirements important to assess.
infographic.paper_title: From local learning to global electronic properties in large-scale systems

title: Does a Trading Policy Need to Know What It Trades? Microstructure Invariance and Zero-Shot Transfer of Execution Policies
authors: Hieu Tran, Hong Yu
abstract: Execution algorithms are calibrated asset by asset, because the queues, trade rates and bid-ask spreads they face differ by orders of magnitude across assets. For reinforcement learning this is zero-shot generalisation across contexts of very different scales, and microstructure invariance proposes a normalisation fixed by theory: measured in each asset's own units of time, size and price, markets look alike. In an exact order-by-order replay of public Nasdaq data, we train policies once, on 954 stocks in 2019, to choose between waiting in the queue and crossing the spread, and evaluate them unchanged on 1,964 unseen stocks in 2020-21, 2,629 stocks in 2025-26, crypto pairs and a second exchange. First, a policy that sees a stock only through its recent trade rate, trade size, spread and price increment (tick) costs within 0.015 spreads per share (a fifth of what learning saves) of a policy whose training data included the stock, and the stock's own history does not help it; it comes within a similar margin of policies trained on the second exchange when every episode counts equally, and within a wider one on crypto. Second, in mean cost before fees, invariant units beat raw units, z-scores and asset descriptors, but by under a basis point: most of their advantage is information and a common cost scale that a learner can also take as plain inputs, and none of the representations tested extrapolates to unseen spread regimes. Third, a near-zero transfer gap to a pooled comparator is weak evidence that a representation is right: we show that such a comparator detects only a small share of what a poor representation loses, and confirm it in synthetic markets and on pendulums.

infographic.key_insight: Trading policies can transfer across assets without knowing their identities, but a small transfer gap does not prove that their market representation is effective.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For execution-system engineers, recent market statistics can support reusable policies, reducing asset-specific calibration; this is financial market research, not materials science.
method: Train reinforcement-learning policies to choose between waiting in a queue and crossing the spread.
Compare microstructure-invariant units with raw units, z-scores and asset descriptors using exact order-by-order replay.
Test unchanged policies across unseen stocks, later periods, crypto pairs and a second exchange.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on 954 stocks in 2019 and evaluated on 1,964 unseen stocks in 2020–21 and 2,629 stocks in 2025–26, a market-statistics-only policy came within 0.015 spreads per share of a policy trained with the test stock included.
infographic.watch_item: No tested representation extrapolated to unseen spread regimes, and invariant units improved mean pre-fee costs by less than one basis point over alternatives.
infographic.paper_title: Does a Trading Policy Need to Know What It Trades? Microstructure Invariance and Zero-Shot Transfer of Execution Policies

title: PolyGPT: A Decoder-Only Transformer for Polymer Electrolyte Design
authors: Tanmay Sarkar Akash, Siddhartha Das
abstract: Designing polymer electrolytes requires control over both material properties and chemical structure. Here, we present PolyGPT, a Transformer with 38.3 million parameters that generates polymer repeat units from optional property targets, requests to include or exclude a specified chemical feature, and an electrolyte-domain condition. Using the model selected by validation loss, we compared unconditional generation with requests for electrolyte-associated structures, a low glass-transition temperature (Tg), or both. Unconditional and electrolyte-only generation achieved structural validity of 99.46% and 99.59%, respectively. However, electrolyte conditioning increased repetition: uniqueness among valid outputs fell from 99.99% to 51.74%. At a Tg target of 246.11 K, we compared generation with and without electrolyte conditioning, and adding the electrolyte condition slightly reduced the predictor-estimated mean absolute error from 26.97 to 26.07 K, but the fraction of all attempts yielding distinct valid polymers within 50 K of the target fell from 82.35% to 32.31%. When we also required absence from the training catalog, these yields were 59.90% and 19.71%, respectively. The lower yield persisted with a tighter 25 K tolerance. Domain conditioning also weakened control of inclusion requests: the mean fraction of attempts producing valid polymers containing the requested chemical feature fell from 94.27% to 31.27%. Across nine checkpoints, earlier models sometimes produced more distinct, catalog-unseen polymers meeting the Tg target: 10,000 checkpoint model with electrolyte conditioning and 30,000 checkpoint model without it. Together, these results show why property error alone is insufficient for evaluating conditional polymer generation. It must be considered alongside repetition, training-catalog novelty, and whether combined design requests are satisfied.

infographic.key_insight: PolyGPT generates highly valid polymer structures, but electrolyte conditioning increases repetition and reduces the yield satisfying combined design requests.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Polymer electrolyte screening should prioritize distinct, valid, target-matching candidates absent from the training catalog rather than property error alone.
method: Use a 38.3-million-parameter decoder-only Transformer to generate polymer repeat units.
Condition generation on optional property targets, chemical-feature inclusion or exclusion, and electrolyte domain.
Compare conditioning strategies and nine checkpoints using validity, uniqueness, catalog novelty, and request satisfaction.
infographic.evidence_signal: At a Tg target of 246.11 K, electrolyte conditioning slightly improved predictor-estimated error from 26.97 to 26.07 K, but reduced the fraction of attempts yielding distinct, valid, catalog-unseen polymers within 50 K from 59.90% to 19.71%.
infographic.watch_item: Predictor-estimated Tg agreement does not establish experimental performance, and validation-loss checkpoint selection may not maximize useful candidate yield.
infographic.paper_title: PolyGPT: A Decoder-Only Transformer for Polymer Electrolyte Design

title: Triboelectric nanogenerators across length scales: linking materials, multiscale modelling and applications
authors: MD Tanzib Ehsan Sanglap, Ans Al Rashid, Abdullah Sayam, Injamamul Arief, Andrei G. Shvarts, Lukasz Kaczmarczyk
abstract: Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) convert low-frequency mechanical energy into electricity and enable self-powered sensing. Their performance depends on interactions among material properties, surface morphology, contact mechanics, charge generation and external circuits. This review examines these interactions across length scales to assess how material and interface descriptions support predictive device design. Polymeric, inorganic, composite and natural materials are discussed in relation to charge generation and retention, mechanical compliance, durability and application requirements. Modelling approaches span molecular dynamics and first-principles calculations, rough-surface contact mechanics, device-scale electrostatics and equivalent circuits. Their capabilities are assessed through the inputs they require, the quantities they predict and the experimental evidence used for validation. Particular attention is given to prescribed surface charge density, idealised geometries and nominal contact-area assumptions, which constrain predictions under realistic loading conditions. Applications are organised by macroscale, milliscale and microscale device dimensions to examine requirements for materials, architecture and integration. The review identifies evolving real contact area and contact-dependent charge generation and decay as critical links between interfacial behaviour and electrical output. A staged validation strategy is proposed for contact mechanics, electrostatics and circuit response, with independent testing beyond calibration conditions. These priorities guide the development of multiscale models and reliable TENG systems.

infographic.key_insight: Predictive triboelectric nanogenerator design requires linking evolving real contact area and contact-dependent charge generation and decay to electrical output across length scales.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Connecting materials, interface mechanics and circuit response can guide more reliable mechanical-energy harvesters and self-powered sensors.
method: Review polymeric, inorganic, composite and natural materials for charging, compliance and durability.
Assess molecular, contact-mechanics, electrostatic and circuit models by their inputs, predictions and validation evidence.
Organise applications by device scale and propose staged validation beyond calibration conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a review of model capabilities and experimental validation evidence, but reports no quantitative benchmark or new device-performance result.
infographic.watch_item: Prescribed surface charge, idealised geometry and nominal contact-area assumptions can limit predictions under realistic loading.
infographic.paper_title: Triboelectric nanogenerators across length scales: linking materials, multiscale modelling and applications

title: Interplay of Ni Order and Local Moments in Intercalated NixNbS2
authors: Gaurav Pransu, Naveen Singh Dhami, Wojciech Sas, Yuki Utsumi Boucher, Bruno Gudac, Ana Smontara
abstract: Magnetic ions intercalated into the van der Waals gaps of layered transition metal dichalcogenides provide a system where local moments interact strongly with a metallic host. How the order of the intercalant sublattice affects their magnetism is important but rarely addressed, although disorder is hard to avoid, in particular in thin films and heterostructures. Here this question is examined in single crystals of Ni$_x$NbS$_2$ with $0.10 \leq x \leq 0.57$, whose composition and Ni order were determined by energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy and synchrotron x-ray diffraction. Anisotropic magnetic susceptibility measurements reveal three regimes. Long-range antiferromagnetic order appears only for $0.25 \leq x \leq 0.33$, where the Ni ions form the $2 \times 2$ and $\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3}$ R$30^\circ$ superstructures, and $T_\mathrm{N}$ reaches 96 K at $x = 1/3$. In this range the effective moment, $\approx 2.5 μ_\mathrm{B}$ per Ni, agrees with DFT+$U$ calculations, in which the Ni spin is partly delocalized onto the surrounding S ligands. For $x \leq 0.18$ the dilute, randomly distributed Ni ions remain paramagnetic down to 2 K with a reduced moment. For $x \geq 0.37$, where Ni-Ni contacts are unavoidable, long-range order gives way to a short-range ordered state below 10-15 K with a further reduced moment. As calculations for ordered Ni arrangements find the Ni state nearly independent of $x$, even at $x = 1/2$, the reduction of the moment is attributed to a disorder-enabled reduction of the charge transfer from Ni to the NbS$_2$ layers. The magnetism of Ni$_x$NbS$_2$ is thus governed by the (dis)order of the Ni sublattice rather than by the Ni concentration alone.

infographic.key_insight: Ni sublattice order—not Ni concentration alone—governs local moments and magnetic ordering in intercalated NiₓNbS₂.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling intercalant order may be essential for reproducible magnetism in layered materials, particularly disorder-prone thin films and heterostructures.
method: Measured Ni composition and ordering using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy and synchrotron X-ray diffraction.
Mapped magnetic behavior with anisotropic susceptibility measurements.
Compared effective moments with DFT+U calculations for ordered Ni arrangements.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across single crystals with 0.10 ≤ x ≤ 0.57, long-range antiferromagnetism appeared only at 0.25 ≤ x ≤ 0.33, reaching Tₙ = 96 K at x = 1/3; dilute samples remained paramagnetic to 2 K, while Ni-rich samples showed short-range order below 10–15 K.
infographic.watch_item: Disorder-induced suppression of Ni-to-host charge transfer is an inferred mechanism; its applicability to thin films and heterostructures remains untested here.
infographic.paper_title: Interplay of Ni Order and Local Moments in Intercalated NixNbS2

title: Symmetry-Gated Sliding: Decoupling Interlayer Translation from Polarization Reversal in Boron Nitride Ferroelectrics
authors: Yinan Wang, Teruyasu Mizoguchi
abstract: Electric-field-driven polarization switching in sliding ferroelectrics depends on how local interlayer motion is accommodated by the surrounding structure. Yet the relationship between sliding, domain-wall (DW) propagation, and collective domain evolution under changing vector fields remains unclear. Here, we show that local symmetry governs the coupling between field-induced forces and interlayer sliding, while DW connectivity determines how local motion contributes to net domain conversion. These effects are examined across three structural scales, from monodomains and isolated DWs to reconstructed moire networks. We investigate bilayer hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) using molecular dynamics with a machine-learning interatomic potential that incorporates field-dependent electric enthalpy. An initially monodomain bilayer switches through directional wrinkling and interlayer sliding, while the barrier along a constrained flat path remains finite. Pre-existing DWs propagate with velocities governed by their shear and tensile character, and an additional in-plane field tunes wall velocity and width according to its orientation. In reconstructed triangular moire networks, shared junctions and boundary curvature mediate domain evolution and recovery after field removal or reversal. Most strikingly, a rotating in-plane field translates the layers and displaces the moiré nodes by approximately 1 AA yet leaves the AB/BA domain-area ratio without detectable change, because threefold connectivity cancels the contributions of individual walls. We term this response polarization-silent sliding. These results distinguish local sliding, DW translation, and net domain conversion as different responses to electric fields and establish how local structural symmetry and DW connectivity shape their selective control.

infographic.key_insight: Local symmetry and domain-wall connectivity let bilayer h-BN slide under electric fields without necessarily reversing its net polarization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Separating interlayer motion from polarization switching could enable selective electrical control of mechanical and ferroelectric responses in layered devices.
method: Molecular dynamics with a machine-learning interatomic potential incorporating field-dependent electric enthalpy.
Compare monodomains, isolated domain walls, and reconstructed moiré networks.
Apply changing vector electric fields to probe sliding, wall motion, and domain conversion.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show that a rotating in-plane field shifts moiré nodes by approximately 1 Å without detectable change in the AB/BA domain-area ratio, attributed to cancellation across threefold-connected walls.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports simulation evidence; experimental validation and sensitivity to defects, substrates, and finite-size effects remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Symmetry-Gated Sliding: Decoupling Interlayer Translation from Polarization Reversal in Boron Nitride Ferroelectrics

title: Conformationally frustrated epitaxy at heteromolecular interface
authors: Jakub Planer, Pavel Procházka, Tomáš Krajňák, Veronika Stará, Daniela Hrubá, Zdeněk Endstrasser
abstract: Precise control of molecular heteroepitaxy offers a route to multilayer architectures with well-defined interfaces. However, the role of intramolecular flexibility in epitaxial matching remains insufficiently understood. Here, we investigate the heteroepitaxy of intact 1,3,5-tris(4-carboxyphenyl)benzene (BTB) on a molecular $δ$-layer composed of fully deprotonated BTB molecules on Ag(111). Combining scanning tunneling microscopy, low-energy electron microscopy and diffraction, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and density functional theory, we identify the key interactions controlling molecular packing and epitaxial growth. We show that intermolecular bonding motifs are preserved on the molecular template, but their lattice parameters and molecular conformations change as compared to a silver surface. Individual molecules exhibit distinct appearances in scanning tunneling microscopy, consistent with site-dependent conformational variations identified by theory. Our calculations reveal that the competition between molecule-substrate interactions and conformational energy produces different compromise geometries, resulting in conformational frustration at the epitaxial interface. Crucially, constraining BTB into a planar geometry changes the preferred lateral adsorption positions, demonstrating that molecular flexibility directly modifies the energetic preferences for epitaxial registry. Comparison with more rigid molecular overlayers further supports this interpretation. Our findings reveal that molecular flexibility contributes to epitaxial matching by allowing unfavorable molecule-substrate interactions to be compensated by energetically favorable conformations while preserving the intermolecular network.

infographic.key_insight: Molecular flexibility reshapes epitaxial registry by balancing molecule–template interactions against conformational energy while preserving intermolecular bonding networks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accounting for molecular conformation could improve the design of multilayer molecular architectures with controlled interfaces.
method: Studied intact BTB on a fully deprotonated BTB δ-layer supported by Ag(111).
Combined scanning tunneling microscopy, low-energy electron microscopy and diffraction, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy.
Used density functional theory to compare flexible and planar-constrained adsorption geometries.
infographic.evidence_signal: Site-dependent microscopy appearances agree with calculated conformational variations, and planar constraints change the predicted preferred lateral adsorption positions.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract establishes the mechanism for BTB on a specific molecular template; its generality across other molecules and interfaces remains to be tested.
infographic.paper_title: Conformationally frustrated epitaxy at heteromolecular interface

title: Equivariant Deep Learning in Direct-Product Space for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction
authors: Shi Yin, Zujian Dai, Xinyang Pan, Lixin He
abstract: Most existing equivariant architectures for Hamiltonian prediction propagate features in direct-sum spaces of irreducible spherical tensors, whereas the target Hamiltonian is naturally an operator block in a direct-product representation over local orbital and spin bases. This representation mismatch fragments contiguous Hamiltonian blocks, obscures direct manipulation of orbital couplings, and organizes features into irregular angular-momentum components that require numerous transformations and are poorly aligned with efficient hardware execution and memory management. To address both the representation mismatch and computational bottleneck, we propose DP-Learner, an equivariant learning framework that performs message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like operator blocks in the direct-product space. Theoretically, we propose Lie-generator-based directional embedding and invariantly weighted left--right products and contractions that preserve equivariance to SO(3), SU(2), and spatial inversions, without explicit Clebsch--Gordan decomposition or inverse reconstruction. Methodologically, we instantiate this principle as a Transformer architecture, in which Hamiltonian-like feature matrices or tensors evolve through equivariant operators in the direct-product space, while non-linear invariant scalar routing controls structured gating over matrix units, directional propagation, attention, and environment-embedded context interactions. We further construct MP-HAM-110K, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset comprising more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements with both Hamiltonian and wavefunction data. Experiments on MP-HAM-110K and Materials-HAM-SOC demonstrate that DP-Learner dramatically improves Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency over the state-of-the-art method.

infographic.key_insight: DP-Learner predicts electronic-structure Hamiltonians directly as symmetry-preserving operator blocks, avoiding fragmentation into irreducible spherical-tensor components.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Direct-product representations align learned features with orbital and spin couplings, potentially reducing transformations and improving computational efficiency.
method: Pass messages over Hamiltonian-like matrices or tensors in a direct-product-space Transformer.
Use Lie-generator directional embeddings and equivariant products and contractions without explicit Clebsch–Gordan decomposition.
Control gating, attention, directional propagation, and environment interactions with invariant scalar routing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors introduce MP-HAM-110K with over 110,000 structures spanning 68 elements and report improved accuracy and inference efficiency on it and Materials-HAM-SOC, without numerical results in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: Practical speedups and memory demands should be checked across orbital-basis sizes and hardware configurations.
infographic.paper_title: Equivariant Deep Learning in Direct-Product Space for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction

title: Non-trivial topological spin-polarized surface states induced nonreciprocal transport in the hourglass semimetal
authors: Zahir Muhammad, Ghulam Hussain, Zia ur Rehaman, Rajibul Islam, Igor Antoniazzi, Muhammad Ismail Khan
abstract: Quantum materials such as topological semimetals have gained consummate interest due to their exotic band crossings and protected surface states. In particular, Ta$_3$GeTe$_6$ has emerged as a prototypical hourglass Dirac semimetal, as confirmed by both experimental and theoretical analysis. The ARPES confirms the topological hourglass-type band dispersions and Rashba-type band, while Hall measurements reveal a high hole carrier concentration and nonreciprocal transport behavior. These findings are further supported by a phenomenological toy model, which predicts a nonreciprocal resistance, consistent with the observed direction-dependent magnetoresistance. Furthermore, the Raman spectroscopy uncovers two-fold and four-fold phonon symmetries drag of highly anisotropic phonons, which establishes symmetry-dependent resistance. DFT calculations reveal Dirac-like and hourglass Dirac band crossings near the Fermi level for the bulk, with Rashba-type spin splitting induced by the surface inversion-symmetry breaking, leading to spin-polarized surface states. The combined experimental and theoretical results demonstrate that Ta$_3$GeTe$_6$ hosts a non-trivial electronic topology, with the inversion-symmetry breaking at the surface as the driver of this nonreciprocal transport behavior.

infographic.key_insight: Ta₃GeTe₆ hosts topological hourglass bands and spin-polarized surface states, with surface inversion-symmetry breaking implicated in nonreciprocal transport.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its direction-dependent resistance could inform anisotropic electronic and spintronic devices, though device performance is not established.
method: ARPES and Hall/magnetotransport measurements probe electronic bands and transport.
Raman spectroscopy characterizes anisotropic phonon symmetries.
DFT and a phenomenological toy model connect surface spin splitting with nonreciprocal resistance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports ARPES-observed hourglass and Rashba-type bands, direction-dependent magnetoresistance, and supporting DFT and toy-model results, without quantitative performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The surface-state contribution to nonreciprocal transport needs quantitative isolation from bulk conduction before device-level claims can be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: Non-trivial topological spin-polarized surface states induced nonreciprocal transport in the hourglass semimetal

title: Complex Martensitic Microstructures in ${\rm Ti}_{76}{\rm Nb}_{22}{\rm Al}_{2}$
authors: John M. Ball, Francesco Della Porta, Tomonari Inamura
abstract: We analyze the unusual microstructure resulting from the cubic to orthorhombic phase transformation in the shape-memory alloy ${\rm Ti}_{76}{\rm Nb}_{22}{\rm Al}_{2}$. This seems to represent an approximate experimental realization of a deformation having a finite number of incompatible deformation gradients, which has been known to exist only as a theoretical possibility. Because the middle eigenvalue $γ$ of the transformation strain is very close to 1, the phase transformation in this alloy takes place via nucleation of exact austenite-martensite interfaces rather than, as usual for other alloys, by classical austenite-martensite interfaces separating the austenite from a finely-twinned laminate of martensite. According to the moving mask approximation of Della Porta this leads to the question whether a microstructure can be formed from the set $H$ of the twelve matrices ${\mathbf V}_i$ on the martensite energy wells that are rank-one connected to the identity, even though these matrices are mutually incompatible. We show that when $γ=1$ and the transformation is volume preserving, such a microstructure is possible that does not deform the grain boundary. This is a consequence of $H$ forming a degenerate $T_{12}$ configuration in the sense of Kirchheim. In fact there are such microstructures supported on just 8 of the 12 matrices in $H$. However there is no deformation satisfying the same boundary condition whose gradient belongs to $H$ almost everywhere. An additional prediction, confirmed experimentally, is that the macroscopic deformation gradient equals the identity everywhere. We also analyse the approximate compatibility of the ${\mathbf V}_i$. Although mutually incompatible, they are nearly compatible, with some pairs much more nearly compatible than others, these pairs corresponding to interfaces that are more frequently observed.

infographic.key_insight: Mutually incompatible martensitic states in Ti76Nb22Al2 can support a boundary-preserving microstructure through a degenerate T12 configuration, despite admitting no exact deformation with gradients restricted to those states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The analysis links transformation-strain compatibility to observed interfaces and macroscopic shape preservation in a shape-memory alloy.
method: Apply the moving mask approximation to 12 martensitic matrices rank-one connected to austenite.
Analyze a degenerate T12 configuration under unit middle eigenvalue and volume preservation, including support on only 8 matrices.
Assess pairwise near-compatibility against observed interface frequencies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experimental confirmation of an identity macroscopic deformation gradient and more frequent observation of interfaces between more nearly compatible pairs.
infographic.watch_item: The existence result assumes an exactly unit middle eigenvalue and volume preservation; it does not provide an exact deformation whose gradient lies in the finite matrix set almost everywhere.
infographic.paper_title: Complex Martensitic Microstructures in ${\rm Ti}_{76}{\rm Nb}_{22}{\rm Al}_{2}$

title: Reversible Interchain Associations Dominate Plateau Elasticity in Conjugated Polymers
authors: Juncheng Zheng, Xiaobing Zuo, Xiaodan Gu, Shiwang Cheng
abstract: The modulus plateau is widely regarded as a hallmark of topological entanglement in homopolymer melts and has been used to identify entanglement in semiflexible conjugated polymers. Using regiorandom poly(3-alkylthiophenes) as a model system, we show that their plateau elasticity relaxes through an Arrhenius process decoupled from segmental and terminal dynamics, reorganizes persistently under mechanical perturbation, and varies systematically with side-chain length. These behaviors are hard to reconcile with a purely topological-entanglement picture and instead support a transient network dominated by reversible interchain associations, consistent with π-π interactions between conjugated backbone segments. The results thus demonstrate that plateau elasticity alone does not uniquely identify topological entanglement in conjugated polymers. More broadly, they identify the strength and lifetime of interchain association as molecular design parameters linking backbone packing to stress relaxation, viscoelastic properties, and processability in conjugated polymers, complementing their established role in electronic structure and charge transport.

infographic.key_insight: Plateau elasticity in regiorandom poly(3-alkylthiophenes) is dominated by reversible interchain associations rather than uniquely indicating topological entanglement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tuning interchain association strength and lifetime offers a route to controlling stress relaxation, viscoelasticity, and processability in conjugated polymers.
method: Use regiorandom poly(3-alkylthiophenes) as a model system.
Compare plateau relaxation with segmental and terminal dynamics.
Probe responses to mechanical perturbation and side-chain length.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports Arrhenius plateau relaxation decoupled from segmental and terminal dynamics, persistent reorganization under mechanical perturbation, and systematic side-chain-length dependence.
infographic.watch_item: The results support associations consistent with π–π interactions, but the abstract does not establish their microscopic origin definitively or demonstrate generality across conjugated polymers.
infographic.paper_title: Reversible Interchain Associations Dominate Plateau Elasticity in Conjugated Polymers
